title: H.E.R.O.
subtitle: A rescue beneath the surface
body: H.E.R.O. is John Van Ryzin's rescue adventure, published by Activision for the Atari 2600 in March 1984. Volcanic activity has trapped miners underground, and Roderick Hero descends through the shafts to reach them. His equipment defines the journey: a propeller backpack carries him through the air, a helmet laser deals with creatures, and dynamite opens blocked passages. Every rescue combines finding a route with controlling the small figure precisely enough to survive the mine's narrow spaces and dangerous walls.

Roderick can rise, move sideways and hover, making the passages navigable in several directions. His power supply steadily falls once movement begins, so a hesitant journey also consumes the time available for rescue. Six sticks of dynamite are supplied for each level. Their fuses briefly illuminate dark rooms before an explosion clears an obstacle. Touching a lantern can extinguish it, changing the visibility of a familiar space. Spiders, snakes and glowing magma walls make a controlled landing as important as the next burst of flight.

Van Ryzin developed the idea after early testing of his Cosmic Commuter project prompted a change of direction. Comic-book superheroes helped inspire the rescuer, but the game's powers are expressed through practical equipment and clear limitations. The backpack frees movement from a sequence of ladders and fixed jumps, while energy and explosives keep that freedom under pressure. The result traveled to several computers and consoles after its Atari debut, carrying a compact design in which a single rescued worker provides a complete objective for each descent.
